transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-18 10:00 PT | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Maya Chen, Daniel Park (Redwood) -- Sofia Alvarez, Ethan Bryant, Maya Patel (Aurora Retail)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect): quick run through of cost results, some numbers were noisy, agreed to run more focused tests.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh, we'll kick off — quick agenda: cost econ numbers, caching results, batching tradeoffs, and then action items. can we do a quick roll call?
[00:10] Sofia Alvarez: yep, Sofia here. hi all.
[00:13] Ethan Bryant: Ethan — running a bit later, but I'm here.
[00:16] Maya Patel: Maya P here.
[00:18] Daniel Park: Daniel from Redwood, hi.
[00:22] Maya Chen: great. so last week we shipped the benchmark harness and ran across your sample data set, two configs: hosted rw-std (open model) and dedicated quantized 8-bit. we have three buckets of results to cover.
[00:36] Daniel Park: quick note: the transcription in the spreadsheet has some 'Redwood Ded' typos — ignore that, it's Redwood Dedicated.
[00:42] Sofia Alvarez: ok cool. can we start with the tokens per dollar numbers? that's our priority.
[00:48] Maya Chen: sure. so top-line, with default batching (batch size 8, concurrency 16) on the dedicated quantized variant we saw about ~1,100 tokens/sec per $1 of GPU time in our normalized model. hosted variant was lower ~650 tokens/sec/$ because of multi-tenant overhead and slightly different kernel paths. these are normalized tokens/sec/$ — mm — so what that means is for your recommendation workload you can expect dedicated to be 1.6-1.8x cheaper per token for most steady-state traffic.
[01:25] Ethan Bryant: 1,100 tokens per second per dollar, sorry can you rephrase — I'm trying to map to our monthly spend assumptions.
[01:31] Daniel Park: yeah so in our cost model we take GPU-hour price * utilization and map to tokens processed in that hour. so 1,100 tokens/sec/$ roughly equals about 4M tokens per GPU-hour per dollar in our normalized example — the spreadsheet has the math.
[01:45] Maya Patel: ok, that math helps. what about caching? you mentioned prefix cache.
[01:50] Maya Chen: yes, prefix/KV cache. with your real traffic shape (we used the sample trace you gave), we saw an effective cache hit of ~42% at the prefix level for the top-100 prompts. that translated to a net token cost reduction of ~34% for the P95 request mix during the test. so tokens/sec/$ improved accordingly — i.e., effective tokens/sec/$ jumped from 1,100 to about 1,650 in that scenario because fewer tokens needed generate per request.
[02:20] Sofia Alvarez: hmm 42% seems high, are we sure? some of our queries are randomized.
[02:25] Daniel Park: it's specifically top-100 heavy traffic; if you have a fat tail the overall hit rate will drop. we simulated both top-heavy and long-tail — top-heavy saw 40-45% hits; long-tail dropped to ~12-15% hits.
[02:38] Ethan Bryant: so we should probably provide a 7-day real traffic sample so you can run the same calculation — we'll action that.
[02:45] Maya Chen: perfect, that's in the next steps.

[02:50] Maya Chen: batching — tradeoffs: when we increase batch size from 8 to 32 we observed throughput (tokens/sec) up ~2.3x, and tokens/sec/$ improved similarly, but P95 latency jumped from ~260ms to ~720ms for individual requests. so for latency-sensitive flows (checkout suggestions) we recommend smaller batch sizes and a dedicated low-latency pool. for bulk offline scoring or non-interactive fan-out, larger batches make sense.
[03:22] Sofia Alvarez: that matches our concern. checkout suggestions are very latency sensitive. how easy is it to route those to a low-latency pool?
[03:29] Daniel Park: you can tag routes and have smart routing policies — we can set a small dedicated pool with batch size 4, concurrency tuned, and a larger cost-optimized pool for async. fallback will automatically route on capacity constraints.
[03:40] Maya Patel: any material difference for quantization? we saw quality drop for some prompts last week.
[03:44] Daniel Park: yes, quantization to 8-bit improved tokens/sec/$ by another ~20% vs fp16 in our tests, but you may see accuracy regressions on very sensitive prompts. we have a mixed strategy: keep a small fp16/float pool for critical flows and quantized for bulk. plus, we can run a small eval suite on your top-500 prompts to quantify quality delta.
[04:03] Sofia Alvarez: please do that eval. we'll need numbers to present to procurement.

[04:10] Ethan Bryant: can you walk me through the numbers in the cost spreadsheet? there's a cell for 'cache saving multiplier' and I'm not sure of the assumptions.
[04:17] Maya Chen: yeah the multiplier uses measured cache hit * average prefix length saved. so the saving = hit_rate * avg_prefix_tokens_saved / total_tokens_per_request. we applied conservative avg_prefix_tokens_saved = 45 tokens for your top prompts. it's adjustable — if your sample shows larger prefixes the savings increase.
[04:36] Maya Patel: we can check that, some of ours have ~80 token templates for product description prompts.

[04:42] Daniel Park: one more point on batching: batching increases kernel efficiency and amortizes KV cache overhead, but it increases tail latency and queueing. also for multi-tenant hosted pools we apply additional safety headroom which reduces effective batch packing a bit. that's why hosted numbers were lower.

[05:02] Sofia Alvarez: what's the expected improvement if we add persistent prefix cache across requests? is that the same as KV cache?
[05:08] Daniel Park: yes persistent KV cache is similar; the difference is whether it's per-session or shared across requests. shared KV cache gave us the 34% reduction earlier on top-heavy traffic. per-session helps personalization but has lower reuse across users.
[05:21] Ethan Bryant: any security implications of shared cache? e.g., PII or sensitive parts ending up in cache?
[05:27] Maya Chen: good question — we recommend token-level masking or canonicalization before caching, and we can scope cache keys to non-sensitive prompt parts. we'll also provide our security whitepaper and SOC2 docs.
[05:36] Sofia Alvarez: thanks. we'll need the SOC2 docs; I filed that as an action item.

[05:40] Maya Chen: ok, on the live tests we ran last night, the dedicated pool hit 68% utilization at 100 rps with batch size 16. throughput was stable. we saw some variance crossing over to 180-200 rps where tail latencies increased; that's expected without autoscaling headroom.
[05:58] Daniel Park: we can propose autoscaling rules — keep baseline capacity at 120 rps and allow 2x burst with 90s cooldown. that keeps P95 under your target for most spikes.

[06:08] Ethan Bryant: what's price sensitivity on burst capacity? if we reserve more capacity we'll pay more.
[06:12] Maya Chen: reserved (Dedicated) vs autoscale costs: reserved monthly commit gives better unit rates and predictable spend. bursting on top of reserved incurs burst pricing; our cost model shows reserved commitments reduce effective tokens/sec/$ by ~25% vs pure on-demand at your target commit level. we can simulate different commit points in the spreadsheet.

[06:32] Sofia Alvarez: perfect. about the eval you mentioned earlier for quantization — what's the run cadence?
[06:36] Daniel Park: we'll run the top-500 prompt eval across fp16 and 8-bit quantized and produce per-prompt delta metrics: F1/ROUGE-ish or heuristic score, and also human spot-checks for top 50. should take ~48 hours once we have the prompt set.

[06:50] Maya Patel: we'll export and share prompts by tomorrow.

[06:54] Maya Chen: great. final quick recap of the numbers: baseline dedicated quantized: ~1,100 tokens/sec/$; with prefix cache (top-heavy) ~1,650 tokens/sec/$; hosted ~650 tokens/sec/$. batching up to 32 gives ~2.3x throughput but P95 jump from ~260ms to ~720ms. quantization appx +20% tokens/sec/$ vs fp16, with potential quality delta we need to measure.
[07:20] Ethan Bryant: ok those are good headlines. please put the spreadsheet in the shared drive with assumptions annotated.
[07:25] Maya Chen: will do. Daniel, any other technical notes?
[07:28] Daniel Park: just that the KV cache TTL we used in the test was 6 hours; shorter TTLs drop hit rate. also we instrumented cache hit logs which we'll share — they include anonymized keys.
[07:38] Sofia Alvarez: thanks. one last ask — can we get an E2E cost run with our 7-day traffic profile that includes network egress and storage?
[07:46] Maya Chen: yes, we'll include network and storage assumptions; network egress in-hosted varies by region but we'll add those numbers and a sensitivity column.

[07:54] Maya Patel: timeline for next call? same time next week?
[07:57] Maya Chen: yes same time next week, and we'll aim to have cache logs, quantization eval, and updated spreadsheet before then.

[08:04] Maya Chen: ok thanks everyone, meeting adjourned.
